title: Philosophy for children: wondering, questions and good reasons
audience: a child in grades K–5 working with an adult helper who reads along
purpose: Wonder out loud about big questions with a grown-up (what is real, what is fair, what makes you you, whether animals think, what a friend is, and where numbers are) while learning to ask good questions, give reasons, listen to other views and change your mind for a good reason.
primary_reading: Teaching Children Philosophy (Prindle Institute for Ethics)

weeks.1: Wondering: what is a big question?
weeks.5: What is real? Dreams, pretend and make-believe
weeks.6: Same and different: what makes you you?
weeks.9: Do animals think? Minds and feelings
weeks.10: Numbers, names and things you cannot touch
weeks.12: Changing your mind for a good reason

blocks.deliverable: Say or write five questions about a picture book and circle the big ones.
Give one reason for and one against an answer to a big question.
Draw yourself as a baby and now, and say what stayed the same.
Week 7 midterm; act out a fair and an unfair way to share.
Talk about whether a pet can be happy and why.
Tell about a time you changed your mind and why.
Submit the project; take an unseen 30 minute final in week 14.

project: Big-question circle: choose a picture book, write three big questions about it with your helper, hold a family "philosophy circle" where everyone gives a reason, and draw or tell what you think now and one good reason someone gave that was different from yours.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
